items.name: writer-001
items.title: Книга: 3D-обложка, которая открывается, форматы и счётчик страниц
items.description: Секция книги писателя: обложка в 3D (perspective, корешок, тень, стопка страниц по краю), при наведении или нажатии открывается на первую страницу с буквицей. Справа описание, факты и переключатель «бумага / электронная / аудио», который меняет цену, подпись и кнопку. Внизу полоса «прочитано читателями: N страниц» тикает каждые пару секунд.

props.title: Rooms We Never Lived In
props.subtitle: Twenty-two essays on houses, cities and what we carry with us
props.author: Vera Kholodova
firstPage: The first house I remember was not ours. We rented it from a woman whose surname sounded like a river, and she came on Thursdays to see whether the ficus plants were alive.
The rooms were enormous, as in a film, and spoke in echoes. I thought it was the house answering.
props.lede: About flats we rented, houses we never moved into, cities where we spent one summer. Essays written over six years in four countries and one kitchen.

formats.name: E-book
formats.note: epub and pdf, a link by email within a minute

formats.note: read by the author, 6 h 40 min

items.name: writer-002
items.title: Архив текстов: крупный список, превью у курсора и раскрытие в списке
items.description: Архив эссе или статей: список с крупными заголовками антиквой, при наведении справа выезжают год и время чтения, а за курсором ходит карточка с первой строкой текста. Фильтр по темам — строка курсивных кнопок с счётчиком. «Читать дальше» раскрывает фрагмент прямо в списке (grid-template-rows 0fr → 1fr) с буквицей и ссылкой «читать целиком».

props.title: Archive
props.lede: Seven years of essays. The short ones last one stop, the long ones the whole way home. Hover: I'll show the first line.

texts.title: A city that sleeps on its side
texts.firstLine: Tbilisi goes to sleep not by the clock but by the slope: the upper streets go dark first.
excerpt: Tbilisi goes to sleep not by the clock but by the slope: the upper streets go dark first, then the ones clinging to them by their balconies, and only towards three — the embankment, where someone keeps laughing by the water.

I lived there one winter and learned to tell floors apart by sound. The upper ones creak. The middle ones sing in the morning, because early risers live there. The lower ones are silent and smell of bread.

texts.title: My grandmother's squared notebook
texts.firstLine: There is not a single date in the notebook, but there are butter prices for eleven years.
excerpt: There is not a single date in the notebook, but there are butter prices for eleven years. That is how I reconstruct time: here we moved, here I was born, here butter doubled in price and the handwriting got smaller.
She did not keep a diary. She kept house. But read those columns in a row and you get the most honest autobiography I know.

texts.title: What a house sounds like when everyone has left
texts.firstLine: The fridge, it turns out, sighs. I did not know that for thirty-four years.
excerpt: The fridge, it turns out, sighs. I did not know that for thirty-four years, because someone was always home and its sigh got lost in conversation.
An empty house sounds like waiting: a door that has not slammed yet, a kettle not yet put on. It does not keep silent. It holds a pause.

texts.title: Words I cannot translate
texts.firstLine: Everyone translates the Portuguese saudade as “longing”, and everyone lies — by about a third.
excerpt: Everyone translates the Portuguese saudade as “longing”, and everyone lies — by about a third. It has a tenderness longing lacks, and lacks the weight longing has.
I collect such words in a separate file. There are fourteen. One per move, as if the language hands me a word for every suitcase.

texts.title: Balconies
texts.firstLine: A balcony is the only room where the owners do not pretend.
excerpt: A balcony is the only room where the owners do not pretend. There is the bicycle, there are the jars, there dries what guests will never see, and there is the chair where someone thinks in the evenings.
If I wrote guidebooks, I would write them by balconies.

texts.title: A letter to a railway station
texts.firstLine: Dear Ladozhsky, you were the first to see me leaving.
excerpt: Dear Ladozhsky, you were the first to see me leaving. You were not surprised. It is your job.

Since then I recognise cities by their stations: those that greet you with an echo, those that greet you tightly, and those where the platform turns straight into a street, as if the city did not want you lingering on the threshold.

texts.title: On the smell of the photocopier
texts.firstLine: There are smells that vanished together with a profession.
excerpt: There are smells that vanished together with a profession. The photocopier in the library basement smelled of hot paper and ozone, and I went there for the smell more often than for the copies.
Now I know: memory keeps not events but the conditions under which we lived them. The light, the temperature, the smell of toner.

items.name: writer-003
items.title: Чтение по прокрутке: закладка-прогресс, сноски на полях, чернильные подчёркивания

props.title: What a house sounds like when everyone has left
props.source: From the book Rooms We Never Lived In, chapter three
paragraphs: The fridge, it turns out, sighs. I did not know that for thirty-four years, because someone was always home and its sigh got lost in conversation, in the radio, in footsteps down the corridor. Now everyone has left — some for work, some for good — and ==the house started speaking in the voice it had had all along==.

I write it down in a notebook, as I would write down birds. Half past seven: the radiator clicks three times, as if counting[1]. Nine: the stairwell light goes off with the sound of a book being closed. Eleven: ==someone upstairs sets down a cup, and I know the cup is white==.
An empty house sounds like waiting: a door that has not slammed yet, a kettle not yet put on. It does not keep silent — ==it holds a pause==, like a good reader before the last line[2].
I think I understood why people get cats. Not for warmth and not for mice. So that there is one more listener in the house[3] — and so that the fridge's sigh becomes someone's again, not only yours.
notes: It turned out later to be the thermostat. But I kept “counting”.
My reading-aloud teacher used to say: a pause is text too, it just isn't typeset.
No cat ever appeared in this essay. A ficus did.

items.name: writer-004
items.title: Отзывы читателей как заметки на полях страницы с ротацией
items.description: Отзывы для сайта писателя: в центре «страница» книги с фрагментом, буквицей, рамкой и колонтитулом, по обе стороны на полях — рукописные заметки читателей (Caveat), каждая чуть повёрнута и подписана именем и городом. Заметки сменяются по кругу: раз в несколько секунд одна гаснет, и на её место вписывается следующая. На узком экране заметки идут колонкой под страницей.

<Writer004
  pageTitle="Балконы"
  page={["Балкон — единственная комната, в которой хозяева не притворяются."]}
  notes={[{ text: "Читала в метро и проехала свою станцию.", name: "Марина", from: "Казань" }]}
/>
ai.summary: Отзывы как заметки на полях книги: рукописные, повёрнутые, сменяются по кругу вокруг страницы с фрагментом.
preserve: видимых заметок count = min(visible, notes.length, 4); чётные слоты слева, нечётные справа; setInterval помечает слот data-leaving, через 420 мс подменяет индекс — новый li получает key и анимацию появления

страница — article[data-part=page] с order:-1 до 60rem (идёт первой), от 60rem сетка 1fr 38rem 1fr и поля с align-content:space-around

en.title: Reader reviews as rotating notes in a page's margins
en.description: Reviews for a writer's site: a book “page” in the centre with an excerpt, a drop cap, a frame and a folio; on both sides in the margins — handwritten reader notes (Caveat), each slightly rotated and signed with a name and city. The notes rotate: every few seconds one fades and the next from the queue is written in its place. On narrow screens the notes go in a column under the page.

props.title: Notes in the margins
props.lede: What people write in margins, letters and on the metro. The notes change — like readers do.
page: A balcony is the only room where the owners do not pretend. There is the bicycle, there are the jars, there dries what guests will never see, and there is the chair where someone thinks in the evenings.
If I wrote guidebooks, I would write them by balconies. Not by façades — façades lie for money — but by what has been put outside because it did not fit inside.

notes.text: Read it on the metro and missed my stop. Twice.
